- Generalized lower quadrant tenderness (consistent with pelvic inflammatory disease [PID], appendicitis, or colitis),  
- Cervical motion tenderness (a classic sign of PID — indicating inflammation of the parametria and uterosacral ligaments),  
- Purulent cervical discharge (strongly suggestive of gonococcal or chlamydial infection, the most common causes of PID).  

Together, these findings meet the CDC’s clinical diagnostic criteria for PID:  
✅ Lower abdominal tenderness  
✅ Cervical motion tenderness  
✅ Purulent cervical discharge  

No other diagnosis explains this triad as cohesively. While appendicitis or ovarian torsion remain possible, they do not typically cause purulent discharge or cervical motion tenderness. Ectopic pregnancy usually presents with adnexal tenderness/mass and may have vaginal bleeding — but not purulent discharge. The absence of fever and presence of discharge strongly favor an infectious gynecologic etiology.

Given the high specificity of this clinical triad for PID — and the risks of untreated PID (tubal infertility, chronic pain, ectopic pregnancy) — empiric diagnosis and treatment are indicated per guidelines, even without imaging or lab confirmation.

[DIAGNOSIS] Pelvic inflammatory disease
